name: Josiah
bio:
Josiah was named more than three centuries before his birth, in a prophecy spoken by an unnamed man of God from Judah who confronted Jeroboam at the idolatrous altar in Bethel: "A son named Josiah will be born to the house of David. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who now make offerings here, and human bones will be burned on you" (1 Kings 13:1-2). This remarkably specific, long-range prophecy was fulfilled centuries later when King Josiah of Judah, in the course of his sweeping religious reforms, did exactly this — a story told in detail many chapters ahead. In the nearer term, after his grandfather Manasseh's long and wicked reign and his father Amon's brief, equally evil one ended in Amon's assassination, the people of Judah made Josiah king in his father's place following the execution of Amon's killers (2 Kings 21:23-24, 26).

## 📖 Core Story: The Book of the Law Found

Josiah began to reign at eight and reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem; his mother was Jedidah. He did right in the LORD's eyes, following David's example without wavering. In his eighteenth year, he sent Shaphan the scribe to the temple to oversee repair funds; there Hilkiah the high priest discovered the book of the law and gave it to Shaphan, who read it to the king. Josiah tore his clothes on hearing it and sent Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asahiah to consult Huldah the prophetess about it, since the LORD's wrath was clearly kindled against Judah's long neglect of its commands. Huldah confirmed disaster was coming on Jerusalem for its idolatry, but told them that because Josiah's heart had been tender and he had humbled himself and wept, he would die in peace before that disaster arrived (2 Kings 22:1-20).  Chronicles gives this episode a fuller timeline: in the eighth year of his reign, while still young, Josiah began to seek the God of David; in his twelfth year he began purging Judah and Jerusalem of their high places, Asherah poles, and idols, extending the purge into the former territory of Israel — Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and all the way to Naphtali — and burning the bones of pagan priests on their own altars there years before the book of the law was even found. Only after finishing this purge did he turn, in his eighteenth year, to repairing the temple, where the book surfaced. The delegation sent to Huldah appears with two variant names in Chronicles: Achbor son of Michaiah is called Abdon the son of Micah, and Asahiah becomes Asaiah (2 Chronicles 34:1-33).

## 📖 Core Story: Sweeping Religious Reforms

Josiah gathered all Judah and Jerusalem at the temple, read the book of the covenant aloud, and led the people in renewing the covenant with the LORD. He then purged the land completely: burning the vessels made for Baal and the Asherah pole, deposing idolatrous priests, destroying the shrine prostitutes' quarters, defiling Topheth where children had been sacrificed to Molech, removing horses dedicated to sun worship near Nathan-Melech's chamber, tearing down altars Ahaz and Manasseh had built in the temple courts, and defiling the high places Solomon had built for Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom. He destroyed Jeroboam's altar and high place at Bethel, burning human bones on it in direct fulfillment of the centuries-old prophecy against it — while sparing the bones of the prophet who had made that prophecy and the old prophet of Bethel buried beside him. He extended the purge through the former territory of Israel and executed the remaining high-place priests on their own altars (2 Kings 23:1-20).

Josiah then had Judah celebrate a Passover unlike any kept since the days of the judges, and removed mediums, spiritists, idols, and every detectable abomination from the land to fulfill the law found in Hilkiah's book. Scripture says no king before or after him turned to the LORD so completely, yet the LORD's wrath against Judah for Manasseh's provocations did not relent, and Judah's eventual removal from the LORD's sight, like Israel's, remained decreed (2 Kings 23:21-27).

Pharaoh-Necho of Egypt marched to the Euphrates against Assyria, and Josiah went out to confront him, dying at Megiddo. His body was carried back to Jerusalem and buried in his own tomb, and the people made his son Jehoahaz king in his place (2 Kings 23:28-30).

 Chronicles gives this Passover in far greater detail: Josiah personally supplied 30,000 lambs and kids and 3,000 bulls from his own flocks for the people's offerings, while his officials — Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, rulers of the temple, and the Levite chiefs Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethaneel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad — donated thousands more animals for the priests and Levites. The priests and Levites carried out every office exactly as David, Solomon, and the book of Moses had prescribed, while the singers descended from Asaph, under the arrangement of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer, kept their posts throughout. Chronicles declares that no Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of the prophet Samuel (2 Chronicles 35:1-19).

Chronicles also gives a fuller account of Josiah's death: when Necho of Egypt marched up to fight at Carchemish, he sent word to Josiah asking why Judah should interfere, insisting God himself had sent him and warning Josiah not to oppose him. Josiah refused to turn back, disguised himself, and went to fight anyway in the valley of Megiddo; when archers wounded him, his servants moved him to a second chariot and carried him to Jerusalem, where he died. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned him, and the prophet Jeremiah composed a lament for him that became a tradition among Israel's singers (2 Chronicles 35:20-25).
